chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Technology that displaced musicians and the human soul in music
summary: Wilson recalls sound movies putting pit musicians out of work, accepts progress, but says electronics should not replace the instruments that express the soul.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Because if they just separate, Milt -- like what is really good, like I remember, you know, when we started, the sound movie was just beginning, and they played things like Broadway Melody and those musicals, and people were talking with all those big stars whom people had never heard their voices, people like John Gilbert and Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks.

So when the sound movies came in, they heard their voices, but it put out of work all these musicians who had been playing in the pit and accompanied those silent movies, the piano players and the groups that played
for the movies. But the sound movie was technically progressive, so you couldn't stop them, even though our unions got all upset about the pictures.

And then the record industry progressed and replaced the live person. So you've got to make room for the new technology-- and these new electronics is almost miraculous. Like my kids have some games they got for Christmas, these electronic games they play on TV, I don't know -- it's amazing how these things do what they do, with electronics.

So this thing cannot be clamped down and stopped, but it should not be allowed to take over the expression of the human soul, which a wooden violin with some strings and a bow, you can say everything that a human, you can tell the insides of a human being are like with that thing.
And with no electricity. So it shouldn't be allowed to replace these instruments where you can really express your individuality where your soul comes through. This marvelous electrical new thing.
